title: Tokenizer amortization and padding costs — latency scan
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad exploring how tokenization overhead and padding inefficiency affect end-to-end latency for short vs long requests. Trying to quantify where to invest engineering effort: faster tokenizer, pre-tokenization amortization, or smarter padding/bucket batching.

Environment:
- Model: redwood-3b-v1 (fp16), hosted-like configuration on a single GPU node (A100-80GB equivalent).
- Serving runtime: local dev build from pr/1427 (includes experimental async tokenization hook).
- Tokenizer: sentencepiece-like tokenizer running on CPU by default (py binding).
- Worker config: inference workers per node = 8, tokenization worker pool = 4 (configurable).
- Load driver: synthetic client (grpc) sending requests at configurable QPS with random prompt lengths.
- Measurements: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency (client-observed), tokenization time (wall), model-only latency (inference only), tokens/sec throughput.

Experiment matrix (core runs):
1) Baseline: tokenization_on_cpu=true, async_tokenization=false, batch_size=1 (single request concurrency).
2) Amortized-tokenize: tokenization_on_cpu=true, async_tokenization=true (separate pool), batch_size=1 but tokenization overlapping with queueing.
3) Tokenize-on-worker: tokenization_on_cpu=false (tokenize on inference worker thread before model run), batch_size=1.
4) Bucketed-padding: same as Baseline but with dynamic bucketing by seq length (8, 32, 128, 512) and minimal padding.
5) Pre-tokenize-cache: we simulate pre-tokenization for repeated prefixes (cache hit 20%).

Inputs: 4 workload mixes
A) Short-heavy: 80% seq_len=8, 15% seq_len=32, 5% seq_len=128
B) Uniform: 25% for each of 8, 32, 128, 512
C) Long-heavy: 70% seq_len=512, 20% 128, 10% 32
D) Micro-interactions: very short 95% seq_len=4 (chat-like), 5% 32

Raw-ish results (single node summary, medians across 3 runs):
- Baseline / Short-heavy:
  tokenization avg: 3.6ms/request
  model-only p50/p95/p99: 12ms / 28ms / 46ms
  end-to-end p50/p95/p99: 17.8ms / 35.2ms / 60.1ms
  tokens/sec (net): 9.8k tokens/s

- Amortized-tokenize / Short-heavy:
  tokenization avg (overlapped): 3.6ms (same) but overlap reduces wall impact to ~1.1ms on avg
  model-only p50/p95/p99: 12ms / 28ms / 46ms
  end-to-end p50/p95/p99: 15.2ms / 30.8ms / 54.6ms
  tokens/sec: 10.6k tokens/s (≈8% improvement)

- Tokenize-on-worker / Short-heavy:
  tokenization avg moved inside worker: increases variance on model worker (tokenization+model serialized)
  model-only p50/p95/p99: 15ms / 40ms / 85ms (inflated p95/p99)
  end-to-end p50/p95/p99: 18.9ms / 47.3ms / 102.4ms
  tokens/sec: 8.7k tokens/s (worse due to blocking)

- Bucketed-padding / Short-heavy:
  tokenization avg: 3.6ms
  model-only p50/p95/p99: 11.4ms / 25ms / 42ms (smaller sequences avoid padding cost)
  end-to-end p50/p95/p99: 16.0ms / 32.5ms / 55.6ms
  tokens/sec: 11.0k tokens/s (best for short-heavy)

- Baseline / Micro-interactions (seq_len=4 dominant):
  tokenization avg: 2.8ms/request (tokenizer constant overhead more relevant)
  model-only p50/p95/p99: 8ms / 22ms / 40ms
  end-to-end p50/p95/p99: 11.2ms / 26.5ms / 46.1ms
  tokens/sec: 12.6k tokens/s

Key observations (takeaways):
- Tokenization has a relatively-fixed per-request cost (~2.5–4ms) dominated by python binding overhead and subword lookups for short prompts. For short-chat workloads this becomes a significant fraction of p50 latency.
- Overlapping tokenization (async pool) reduces the perceived tokenization impact without requiring moving tokenization into the inference worker. It yielded ~6–10% throughput improvement for short-heavy mixes and reduced p95 by a few ms.
- Moving tokenization into inference worker threads reduces tail behavior for large-seq scenarios because tokenization becomes serialized with model work: p99 worsened dramatically in our config. So avoid blocking tokenization on model threads under high concurrency.
- Bucketing (minimizing padding) gives the largest wins for mixes with many short requests: up to ~12% throughput and consistent reduction in p95/p99. For long-heavy workloads, bucketing helps less (since model time dominates).
- Pre-tokenization cache helps only if there is a non-trivial prefix hit rate. 20% prefix hits gave ~3–4% throughput gain. Benefit scales with repeated prompt patterns (chat system messages, common instructions).

Anomalies / noisy signals:
- On 2026-02-28 run we saw a p99 spike that correlated with kernel-level page faults when the tokenizer process hit a GC stall (CPython). Reproduced by artificially forcing GC pauses (bad). Potential fix: move tokenizer to a small native (Rust) shim or use PyPy / PyO3 bindings to reduce GC pauses.
- One run showed improved performance when tokenization pool size was lowered from 8->4, indicating contention for CPU caches and SSA on the host. Need cpu-affinity experiments.

Quick recommendations (prototype path):
- Short term: enable async_tokenization by default for hosted API; add config to tune tokenization pool size per-node. Immediate wins and low-risk.
- Mid term: implement bucketing by seq-length with small number of buckets (4) and adaptive bucket selection based on rolling histogram. Ship as opt-in.
- Long term: explore a lightweight native tokenizer (Rust or C++) with an FFI that reduces per-request overhead <1ms, and experiment with zero-copy token buffers for GPU-resident token ids to avoid memory copies.

Next steps / experiments to run:
- CPU affinity sweep: pin tokenization workers to dedicated logical cores and measure p95/p99 impact (tickets: JIRA-RI-3299).
- Native tokenizer PoC: benchmark pure tokenization time vs Python binding. Target is <1ms for seq<=8.
- Combined: bucketed + async_tokenization + pre-tokenize cache with realistic chat trace (from telemetry) to estimate real-world wins.

Notes to self (TODOs):
- Add per-request wall traces (tokenization_start/end, enqueue, model_start) to trace pipeline (instrumentation PR).
- Share these preliminary numbers with Zara and Maya; sync to prioritize native tokenizer work if CPU-affinity doesn't close gap.
- Add a microbenchmark harness for tokenization in CI to avoid regressions.

Unresolved questions:
- At what prefix-hit rate does pre-tokenization caching justify the memory/complexity? (simulate heavy reuse scenarios)
- How do these numbers change on lower-tier hardware (T4 / V100) where CPU resources are different?

End of scratchpad.
